title: Which assets need a label
scenario: A travel agency, Harbor & Pine, plans a spring campaign with several AI assets. You decide which ones need disclosure. Use the exhibit. The agency, the assets and the plan are made up for this case. The policy and platform lines are copied from the official pages.
exhibit:
ASSETS (made up for this case):
  A1  Veo 3.1 clip: a realistic video of a surfer on the real beach at a partner
      resort. Nobody filmed it. Posted on YouTube.
  A2  Animated mascot: a cartoon seal sails a paper boat across a fantasy sea.
      Made with AI. Posted on YouTube.
  A3  The title and thumbnail for A1, drafted with AI and finished by a designer.
  A4  "Ask Pine", a chat helper on the agency site. A Claude model answers visitors.
  A5  A teammate's idea: export A1 without metadata, "so no platform adds a label".
  A6  The campaign also runs in the EU.

LINES (copied from the pages):
  YouTube: creators must disclose content that "Generates a realistic scene that didn't actually occur."
  YouTube: "Creators don't need to disclose non-realistic content that's made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor."
  YouTube: "Production assistance, like using generative AI tools to create or improve a video outline, script, thumbnail, title, or infographic" needs no disclosure.
  YouTube: "Disclosing AI content won't limit a video's audience or impact its eligibility to earn money."
  Anthropic Usage Policy: "All consumer-facing chatbots ... must disclose to users that they are interacting with AI rather than a human. This disclosure must be provided at a minimum at the beginning of each chat session."
  European Commission: "Even though adherence to the code is voluntary, the transparency requirements under article 50 of the AI Act are legal obligations."

questions.prompt: Which assets need the YouTube "AI use" disclosure, using the lines in the exhibit?

options.text: A1 only, because it is a realistic scene that never happened
options.explanation: Right. A1 is realistic and shows a real place. A2 is non-realistic, and A3 is production assistance.

options.text: A1 and A2, because both of the clips were made with AI tools
options.explanation: YouTube says non-realistic content made with AI does not need disclosure. A2 is a fantasy cartoon.

options.text: A1, A2 and A3, because AI was used on all three video assets
options.explanation: YouTube lists AI help on a title or thumbnail as production assistance that needs no disclosure.

options.text: None of them, because the agency wrote the captions itself
options.explanation: The duty depends on realistic AI content, not on who wrote the captions. A1 is realistic.

questions.prompt: What do you say about A5, exporting A1 without metadata so that no platform adds a label?

options.text: Do it, because YouTube only ever labels files that carry metadata
options.explanation: YouTube also labels content that its own systems detect as AI. Stripping the data is not a safe way to avoid a label.

options.text: Do it, because disclosing an AI video lowers how many people see it
options.explanation: YouTube says disclosing AI content will not limit a video's audience or its eligibility to earn money.

options.text: Do it, and put a small AI badge on the video instead of disclosing
options.explanation: A badge on the picture does not answer YouTube's AI use question. YouTube asks creators to disclose in YouTube Studio at upload.

options.text: Refuse, and answer Yes to AI use, because the duty stays without metadata
options.explanation: Right. A1 is a realistic scene that never happened, so YouTube requires disclosure. Hiding AI use risks a manual label or penalties.

questions.prompt: What does the Anthropic Usage Policy line mean for A4, the chat helper?

options.text: Add a line to the privacy page, which every visitor can find if they look
options.explanation: The policy asks for disclosure at a minimum at the beginning of each chat session or in the product interface. A line on a separate privacy page is neither.

options.text: Tell each visitor at the start of every chat that they are talking to AI
options.explanation: Right. The policy says the disclosure must be given at a minimum at the beginning of each chat session or in the product interface. A notice at the start of every chat meets that.

options.text: Say it only when a visitor asks outright whether the helper is a bot
options.explanation: The policy does not wait for a question. Consumer-facing chatbots must disclose that they are AI.

options.text: Nothing, because staff read through the helper's answers once every week
options.explanation: Staff review does not replace the disclosure. The policy line has no exception for reviewed chatbots.

questions.prompt: A6: the EU team asks, "Do we need a label by law for A1?" What is the best answer?

options.text: No, because the Code of Practice is voluntary, so all labels are optional
options.explanation: The Commission says the code is voluntary, but the transparency requirements in Article 50 are legal obligations.

options.text: Yes, because the AI Act says that every AI-made file must carry a label
options.explanation: That goes further than the page. Providers must mark outputs in a machine-readable way, and deployers must label deepfakes and certain text. It does not say every AI file needs a visible label.

options.text: Ask a lawyer if A1 is a deepfake under Article 50, and read the guidance
options.explanation: Right. The page says Article 50 duties apply from 2 August 2026 and cover deepfake labels. Whether A1 counts is a legal question.

options.text: No, because only the platform has a duty, while the agency has none at all
options.explanation: The page describes duties for providers and for deployers. An agency that publishes content may be a deployer.
